title: What Krishna told Arjuna first
hook: a warrior drops his bow, and Krishna's first teaching hides a second 'not' inside one word
carry: atman: the real in you never stops being
tomorrow: one hidden a, and two schools read a line opposite ways?

segments.voice: Yesterday, tapas: he had to win against himself, and a king became the seer tradition credits with the Gayatri. Today, a warrior who can't lift his bow, and the first thing Krishna tells him.

Two armies face each other on the field of Kurukshetra, and the best archer on either side sits down in his chariot. Arjuna has looked across and seen his teachers, his cousins, old Bhishma who helped raise him. His bow slips from his hand. I will not fight, he says, and goes quiet. His charioteer is Krishna. In the Gita's telling, Krishna smiles, and begins not with tactics but with this: you grieve for what should not be grieved. Then a line Hindus have loved ever since: nasato vidyate bhavo, nabhavo vidyate satah.
screen: `AN ARCHER SITS DOWN.` → `I WILL NOT FIGHT.` → `KRISHNA SMILES, AND BEGINS.`

segments.voice: Roughly: the unreal never comes to be; the real never stops being. And there's a small puzzle in it worth solving, because it holds the whole teaching. Each half seems to have one not: na. But there are two. Sanskrit turns a word into its opposite with a short a in front: sat, the real; asat, the unreal. When na meets asat, the two a's melt into one long a, and the second not slips out of sight. Na, asatah: nasato. So what is the real that never stops being? Krishna says it in the verses around this one: the Self, the atman, the one who lives in the body. Bodies are born, change and end, the way clothes are worn and set aside. The atman isn't born and doesn't die. Weapons don't cut it; fire doesn't burn it. That's the Gita's first teaching, and it's one reason many Hindu families read the Gita, often chapter two, when someone dies. It doesn't say the loss isn't real. Arjuna's tears are real, and Krishna doesn't mock them. It says the person you love was never only the body you're losing. And once Arjuna has heard it, Krishna turns him back toward what he has to do. In the Gita, grief isn't the end of the road. It's where the teaching starts.
screen: `THE UNREAL NEVER COMES TO BE.` · `NA + ASATAH: A HIDDEN NOT.` · `BODIES, LIKE CLOTHES.` · `ATMAN: NOT BORN, NEVER DIES.` · then, large: `THE REAL NEVER STOPS BEING.`

segments.voice: If you keep a Gita at home, open it to chapter two and read verse sixteen slowly, once. If not, just hold its meaning: the unreal never comes to be; the real never stops being. Then bring to mind one person or thing you're afraid to lose. Don't push the fear away. Set beside it the question Krishna sets beside Arjuna's tears: what here is real, and can't be taken? Then rest with the breath.
Sandhi plainly: where words meet and melt. Today, two short a's melting into one long one, and a second not hiding inside nasato.
For the road: atman, the real in you never stops being. Bodies change like clothes; the Self doesn't. Until tomorrow.

original.note: Sanskrit: of the unreal there is no being (Bhagavad Gita 2.16).

trapdoor: what you thought: nasato is one word in a famous line.
what it means: na, not, plus asatah, of the unreal: the unreal never is, and the real, the atman, never isn't.
what a scholar hears: like vowels join as one long vowel (Ashtadhyayi 6.1.101), so each half holds two negatives; the verse opens Krishna's teaching on the undying Self (Gita 2.11–30).
recall: raja + rishi: a and ri make ar
su + agatam: u turns to v

Gita.meaning: the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna's teaching to Arjuna

nasato.meaning: na + asatah: not, of the unreal

asat.meaning: the unreal; sat, the real, with a short a in front

abhava.meaning: non-being; bhava, being, with a short a in front

atman.meaning: the Self, the one who lives in the body; not born, never dies

Arjuna.meaning: the archer prince Krishna teaches in the Gita

Kurukshetra.meaning: the battlefield where the Gita is spoken

sources.quoted: nasato vidyate bhavo, nabhavo vidyate satah

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.16 (meaning: of the unreal no being, of the real no non-being)
Bhagavad Gita 1.47 and 2.9–2.11 (Arjuna sets down his bow; Krishna, smiling, says he grieves for what should not be grieved)
Bhagavad Gita 2.20–2.23 (the Self is not born and does not die; bodies set aside like worn clothes; weapons do not cut it, fire does not burn it)
Ashtadhyayi 6.1.101 (akah savarne dirghah: like vowels join as one long vowel)
